# Item fit, person fit and item quality {#fit}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* explain what item fit means and why it is always fit *to a model*;
* compute and read the S-X² item-fit statistic and its RMSEA;
* compare an empirical item curve with the model curve;
* flag aberrant response patterns with the Zh person-fit statistic, and say
  what can cause them;
* summarize an item's health for a review meeting.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[item fit](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#item-fit),
[S-X²](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#s-x2),
[empirical item curve](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#empirical-item-curve),
[person fit](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#person-fit),
[Zh](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#zh),
[model fit](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#model-fit).

## The ideas

Chapter \@ref(estimation) asked whether a model fits the test *as a whole*.
Item fit asks the same question one item at a time: does the item's curve
describe how people at different ability levels actually responded?

The most widely used statistic is Orlando and Thissen's **S-X²**
[@orlando2000]. It groups people by their sum score, compares the observed
proportion correct in each group with the proportion the model predicts, and
adds up the squared differences. A small p-value means the item does not
follow the model. Because a test has many items, some will be flagged by
chance, so it is good practice to adjust the p-values (for example with the
Benjamini-Hochberg method) and to look at an effect size too: mirt reports
an RMSEA for each item, where values below about 0.05 mean the misfit is
small in practice.

Item fit is always fit *to a particular model*. An item with an unusually
steep curve fits the 2PL perfectly well but misfits the Rasch model, which
forces all slopes to be equal. A misfitting item is a question, not a
verdict: look at the empirical curve, the content and the key before you
decide.

**Person fit** turns the question around: does a person's response pattern
look like what the model expects of someone at their $\theta$? The **Zh**
statistic [@drasgow1985] is a standardized log-likelihood of the pattern.
Values near zero are typical; large negative values (below about -2) mean
the pattern is unlikely: a strong student who misses easy items, or a weak
one who gets the hardest items right. Causes include careless responding,
guessing, cheating, misaligned answer sheets, fatigue and atypical
instruction. Zh flags a pattern for a closer look; it never proves
misconduct.

## Example 1: the same items under two models

We return to the `SAT12` science items, scored with the corrected key.

```{r data-fit-1}
# SAT12 science items, scored with the corrected key (item 32 keyed 3).
key <- c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,3)
resp <- key2binary(SAT12, key)
```

First, the Rasch model. `gg_itemfit()` plots each item's S-X² RMSEA and marks
the items whose p-value is below `alpha`.

```{r, fig.height = 5}
rasch <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
gg_itemfit(rasch, p_adjust = "BH")
```

`item_table()` puts the classical statistics, IRT parameters, fit and flags
in one table. Here are the items that misfit the Rasch model most:

```{r}
tab_r <- item_table(rasch, p_adjust = "BH")
tab_r[order(tab_r$p.value), c("item", "item_total_r", "location", "S_X2", "df",
                              "RMSEA", "p.value")][1:5, ]
```

The worst-fitting items include items whose item-total correlation is far
from the typical value: either much flatter or much steeper than the common
slope the Rasch model imposes. Now fit the 2PL, which lets the slopes vary:

```{r}
twopl <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
tab_2 <- item_table(twopl, p_adjust = "BH")
c(misfit_rasch = sum(tab_r$p.value < 0.01), misfit_2pl = sum(tab_2$p.value < 0.01))
```

The 2PL removes the misfit. Whether that is the right response depends on
the purpose. A Rasch programme would rather revise or drop the items that do
not fit, because equal slopes give the sum score its simple meaning; a 2PL
programme would keep them.

An **empirical item curve** shows the misfit directly. People are grouped by
their estimated $\theta$, and the observed proportion correct in each group
is plotted against the model curve:

```{r, fig.height = 3.4}
worst <- tab_r$item[which.min(tab_r$p.value)]
gg_empirical(rasch, worst) + gg_empirical(twopl, worst)
```

Under the Rasch model the observed points do not follow the curve; under the
2PL they do. Fit is not the only thing that matters about an item, though.
`item_table()` also flags items that are very easy or very hard, or that
discriminate poorly:

```{r}
tab_2[tab_2$flag != "", c("item", "mean", "item_total_r", "discrimination",
                          "location", "flag")]
```

An **item health card** collects everything about one item on a page, with a
traffic-light status, for item review meetings:

```{r, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 6.5}
weak <- tab_2$item[which.min(tab_2$discrimination)]
item_card(twopl, weak)
```

`item_cards(twopl, file = "cards.html")` writes a card for every item into
one HTML page that reviewers can open in a browser.

## Example 2: finding aberrant response patterns

We simulate a 30-item quiz taken by 1,000 students. Most students respond
according to a 2PL model, but 40 answered at random (careless responding)
and 30 weak students somehow got the ten hardest items right (perhaps they
saw them in advance). We record who is who so we can check the person-fit
statistic.

```{r data-fit-2}
# Simulated 30-item quiz: 930 regular students, 40 random responders and
# 30 weak students who know the 10 hardest items. `type` records which.
set.seed(505)
a <- matrix(rlnorm(30, 0.2, 0.2)); b <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 30)
resp <- simdata(a, matrix(-a * b), N = 1000, itemtype = "2PL")
colnames(resp) <- sprintf("Q%02d", 1:30)
type <- rep(c("regular", "random", "preknowledge"), c(930, 40, 30))
resp[type == "random", ] <- rbinom(40 * 30, 1, 0.5)
weak <- simdata(a, matrix(-a * b), N = 30, itemtype = "2PL",
                Theta = matrix(rnorm(30, -1.2, 0.3)))
weak[, 21:30] <- 1
resp[type == "preknowledge", ] <- weak
```

`augment()` adds each person's score, its standard error and, with
`person_fit = TRUE`, the Zh statistic to the data:

```{r}
mod <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
scores <- augment(mod, person_fit = TRUE)
scores$type <- type
head(scores[, c(".F1", ".se_F1", ".Zh", "type")])
```

How well does Zh separate the groups?

```{r, fig.height = 3.2}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(scores, aes(.Zh, fill = type)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, position = "identity", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -2, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Zh person-fit statistic", y = "Students", fill = NULL) +
  theme_mirtverse()
aggregate(.Zh < -2 ~ type, data = scores, FUN = mean)
```

All of the students with pre-knowledge are flagged: getting the hardest
items right while missing easier ones is very unlikely under the model. Most
random responders are flagged too, because on a 30-item test with a wide
range of difficulties a coin-flip pattern contradicts the model again and
again. Only a handful of regular students fall below -2. Real data are rarely
this clean: aberrance is usually milder, and only part of a test may be
affected (the last items, say, for a student who ran out of time). That is
why Zh is a screening tool: flagged patterns need a human look, and often
other evidence such as response times (see the [response-time
article](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/response-times.html)).

Do the aberrant patterns distort the item parameters? We can check by
refitting without the flagged students and comparing both sets of
difficulties for the ten hardest items with the values used to simulate the
data:

```{r}
clean <- mirt(resp[scores$.Zh >= -2, ], 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
b_all <- coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[21:30, "b"]
b_clean <- coef(clean, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[21:30, "b"]
round(c(error_all = mean(abs(b_all - b[21:30])),
        error_clean = mean(abs(b_clean - b[21:30]))), 3)
```

Here the difference is small, because only 7% of the students are aberrant
and the model is estimated from everyone else. With more contamination, or
with pre-knowledge concentrated on a few items, the damage grows, and
removing flagged cases before calibration is common practice.

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. Plot the empirical curve of the best-fitting item under the Rasch model in
   Example 1. How does it compare with the worst-fitting one?
2. Rerun `gg_itemfit()` for the Rasch model without the p-value adjustment.
   How many more items are flagged? Which result would you report?
3. In Example 2, which value of the Zh cut-off flags at most 5% of the regular
   students? How many students with pre-knowledge does it catch?
4. Write two sentences to a school principal explaining what a flagged
   person-fit statistic means and what it does not mean.
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r, fig.height = 3.4}
best <- tab_r$item[which.max(tab_r$p.value)]
gg_empirical(rasch, best)
sum(item_table(rasch)$p.value < 0.01)
cut5 <- quantile(scores$.Zh[type == "regular"], 0.05)
c(cutoff = unname(cut5),
  caught = mean(scores$.Zh[type == "preknowledge"] < cut5))
```

2. Without adjustment more items are flagged, some only by chance. With 32
   tests, report the adjusted results, and look at the RMSEA to judge size.
4. For example: "This student's pattern of right and wrong answers is unusual
   for someone with their overall score, so we checked it more closely. It is
   not evidence of cheating on its own; it can also come from guessing,
   fatigue or a mismatch between what was taught and what was tested."

</details>

## Further reading {-}

Orlando and Thissen [-@orlando2000] introduced S-X². Drasgow, Levine and
Williams [-@drasgow1985] introduced the standardized person-fit index Zh.
de Ayala [-@deayala2022] discusses item and person fit at length.
